ChatGPT is eyeing Gemini’s job on Android, with ability to make calls, send texts, and more

It could also peek at your screen to answer your questions better.

Stephen Radochia / Android Authority

TL;DR

• OpenAI is testing more features for the ChatGPT app on Android to let it control parts of your phone.

• Based on the evidence we found, ChatGPT could make calls, send or receive SMSes, control media playback, and even view what’s on your screen.

• OpenAI is also testing broader utility for Dots to accomplish more on Android.

If you’re fond of ChatGPT and prefer it over Gemini, you can already assign it as the default assistant on your Android devices. Even then, its current abilities remain limited to Voice mode and responding to your queries in text only. But now, OpenAI could be working on giving ChatGPT more control on your Android device — with your permission.

OpenAI appears to be working on deeper ChatGPT integration in Android, where the assistant could soon do more than just chat with you. We’ve dug up references to ChatGPT’s upcoming abilities to make calls, send text messages, control media, and so much more.

ChatGPT could make calls and reply to messages

In version 1.2026.328, we found strings associated with permissions that ChatGPT could request before looking through your call history, placing calls for you, looking up your contacts, or reading and sending text messages.

Code

I need access to your phone’s contacts to finish this lookup.

Let ChatGPT read recent calls on this phone, including phone numbers and saved names.

Allow this workspace to place calls from your phone?

Allow this workspace to read and send text messages on your phone?

Let ChatGPT place phone calls from this phone when you ask.

It could control media playback

Along with these, certain other strings hint at the possibility of letting ChatGPT find and control media on your phone using notifications access. ChatGPT could play, pause, or skip tracks on Android devices, as per the following strings.

Code

Let ChatGPT find and control media playing on this phone

Allow this workspace to find and control media playing on your phone?

Allow notification access for ChatGPT in Android Settings, then return to this request to continue.

Pause, resume, or skip tracks on this phone. ChatGPT uses Android notification access to control playback.

Another permissions-related string reveals ChatGPT might be able to look up local media players, determine their existing states, and the actions they allow. Along with that, ChatGPT could identify the artist and track, potentially to learn your preferences or recommend music. However, it may not be able to directly launch media players or play or resume a particular track if that information isn’t visible in notifications.

Code

Read the current local media players on this Android phone, their playback state, supported actions, and available title and artist.

Resume means play the existing session; this tool does not open an app or choose new music.

After a verified resume, finish without any spoken follow-up so you do not interrupt the music.

When used, ChatGPT could also verify whether the outcome matches what was desired. However, there may not be a verbal confirmation or follow-up since that might interrupt media playback.

Or read what’s on your screen

Besides controlling media playback and making calls or sending texts for you, ChatGPT might be able to view what’s on your screen and use it as context to help you with queries.

Code

Read what is currently visible on this Android phone's screen. Call this tool again for every new question about the current screen, including follow-ups

Ask about your screen

Turn on “Use screen and app data”

The strings related to this feature suggest ChatGPT could pull up a new screenshot in response to every follow-up question about what’s on your screen.

And connect to Dots

Certain other permissions we spotted cite a Dot card, likely referring to ChatGPT’s eponymous always-on agent that executes tasks without requiring you to keep the app active.

Code

Use the same Dot card. After granting notification access in Android Settings, return to that card and tap Connect if prompted, or Continue.

With reference to Dots, we also see two configurations in the code:

Code

allowedWhileLocked

useDotAsAssistant

The former of the two suggests ChatGPT might be able to hail Dots even when the phone is locked, while the latter hints at the possibility of allowing users to use a particular Dot as the digital assistant on their phone.

The extent to which Dots might have access to Android devices remains unclear. Beyond these strings — and speculations based on the text, we don’t have evidence showing exactly how these features could function. We’re unsure when we might be able to see it in action, but we’ll share updates whenever it happens.

Shoppers rate the Galaxy A37 4.4 out of five stars on Amazon, and this discount makes it an easy recommendation for anyone who wants a capable Samsung phone without the premium price.

•

•

•

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

TL;DR

• TRIMUI is now shipping the Brick Hammer Pro U Android handheld.

• The new handheld offers a metal design, Snapdragon G2 Gen 1 chip, 6GB of RAM, and 128GB of expandable storage.

• Expect to pay $249.89 for the Brick Hammer Pro U.

TRIMUI has quickly made a name for itself as one of the best brands if you’re looking for a cheap Linux-powered handheld. The company announced the Brick Pro earlier this year, but this was also accompanied by the more premium Brick Hammer Pro U. Thankfully, the waiting is over as you can finally buy the latter device.

The Brick Hammer Pro U is now available to purchase via the TRIMUI website (h/t: RetroDodo), complete with a $249.89 price tag. For what it’s worth, the product page previously listed a $293.99 price. Then again, the handheld was originally expected to launch with a sub-$200 price tag. But much like other consumer electronics, it was affected by the AI-induced RAM crisis.

TRIMUI Store

The official blog adds that this initial batch is limited to 3,000 units and is shipping now. It’s unclear whether the company will be producing more units if this initial batch is sold out. Nevertheless, TRIMUI is also offering a free Basic Protection Bundle with each purchase. This includes a console lanyard, a screen protector, a protective shell, and a carrying bag.

Otherwise, the Brick Hammer Pro U stands out from most other TRIMUI handhelds by running Android out of the box rather than Linux. The device ships with Android 15, along with a Snapdragon G2 Gen 1 chipset, 6GB of RAM, 128GB of expandable storage, and a 5,000mAh battery. This vertical-style handheld also packs a 3.95-inch IPS LCD screen (1,024 x 768, 60Hz), dual analog sticks, and an aluminum design.

In any event, there’s no shortage of vertical Android handhelds for the price. Some of the most prominent rivals include the ANBERNIC RG 477V, the upcoming ANBERNIC RG 47G1, and the MANGMI Air Y series.

items.body: U.S. smartphone shipments fell 9% year-over-year in the third quarter of 2026, and yet Apple grew its share of the market from 50% to 57%, according to the latest U.S. Market Monitor data from Counterpoint Research . Apple was the only major manufacturer to avoid a shipment decline in the quarter. Counterpoint put the wider market decline down to rising memory costs, which hit Android manufacturers hardest at the low end. Thin margins leave little room for these vendors to absorb higher component prices without raising their prices or cutting volume. Samsung held its ground at 25% share, up one point year-over-year, thanks to its flagship Galaxy S and Z series devices and the low-end Galaxy A-series. But it was Motorola that took the biggest hit – its share fell four points to 8% as memory costs squeezed its large low-end lineup, essentially reversing the share growth it posted in the second quarter. Meanwhile, Google's Pixel 11 launch was not strong enough to prevent a slight decline in share. Smartphone sales at the Big Three carriers already declined 4% year-over-year in Q3, and Counterpoint similarly expects weak Q4 sales as consumers increasingly time purchases around the best deals. Last month, Counterpoint's global third-quarter data likewise showed Apple gaining share in a shrinking smartphone market . items.summary: It could make Collections even more useful.

First look: Google Play Store’s new ‘Today’ feed could pull content from your favorite apps

It could make Collections even more useful.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 6:37 AM ET

•

•

Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Google is working on a new “Today” feed for Collections in the Play Store.

• It combines recommendations from multiple apps into a single feed.

• Users can also choose which apps contribute content to the feed.

It’s been a while since Google first introduced Collections in the Play Store, and the feature has largely remained unchanged, barring some new widgets we spotted the company working on. Although Collections is quite good at organizing content from your installed apps into separate categories, Google is now working on a new feed that brings all of these recommendations together.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

While digging through the latest version of the Google Play Store (v54.4.11), we found evidence of Google working on a new “Today” feed inside Collections. With a bit of tinkering, we managed to enable it on our device. The new tab appears right next to “App Library,” ahead of the existing content categories.

We also spotted a new pop-up that could show up the first time a user opens Collections after the feature rolls out. In the Today feed, you will be able to browse recommendations from multiple apps in one place instead of switching between individual collections. On our test device, the feed showed favorite playlists from Spotify alongside game recommendations from the Play Store.

Google is also adding customization options for the new Today feed. Just like with other feeds in Collections, you can choose which apps contribute content to the Today feed. The list includes apps like Google Maps, Play Books, Play Store, Spotify, YouTube, and YouTube Music, along with any other app that’s supported in the different collection categories. You can also change the position of the Today tab or remove it from Collections entirely.

The new Today collection isn’t live yet, and we only managed to turn it on with a bit of tinkering. However, it seems to be working as expected. Hopefully, Google will roll it out soon.

items.title: Gemini ran my errands on the Pixel 10 like I was in a sci-fi movie
items.summary: Want to spend your time watching Gemini use your phone?
items.body:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

General technology

Gemini ran my errands on the Pixel 10 like I was in a sci-fi movie

Want to spend your time watching Gemini use your phone?

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 6:30 AM ET

•

•

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

Gemini Intelligence isn’t just a marketing term that Google slaps onto its Pixel phones. It enables a bunch of handy AI features, including task automation — the dream use case for artificial intelligence. A whole bouquet of these automations recently made their way to last year’s Pixel 10 in newer regions, after debuting on the Pixel 11, and I couldn’t keep myself from giving it a go.

Gemini can already work inside a few apps in the backend, but it can now interact with third-party apps just like you do, using the same visual interface. It brings to reality the idea of AI taking over your mundane tasks like a true assistant. After living with Gemini Intelligence on the Pixel 10, I feel like I’ve had a taste of the future.

Readers' poll

Would you use Gemini's task automation instead of navigating apps yourself?

2 votes

Setting up Gemini’s task automations on the Pixel 10

Google

As confusing as it may be, Gemini can interact with other apps in two ways. One is through connectors that let it work in the app in the background without needing to interact with the user-facing interface, but this new automation feature that we are talking about today allows Gemini to work with the same UI that you and I see, with the help of taps and scrolls, to get the job done, opening up Gemini to more third-party apps that don’t yet have a Gemini connector.

While the Pixel 11 series has had the feature since launch, the latest November QPR update introduced the feature to the Pixel 10 series in certain regions (India, Japan, and the UK, in addition to the US). A handful of recent Samsung flagships are also supported, so you need to have one of the compatible devices with the latest update installed to use Gemini’s on-screen automations. Having said that, there was no Gemini setting to flick it on in my case (Google’s official docs say there is), leaving you at Google’s mercy and its erratic server-side rollout, even if you have the latest update installed.

To check whether the feature is available to you, you have to directly ask Gemini to do something in one of the supported apps — we recently uncovered a hidden list of apps that Gemini supports for task automations, and that is also the only way to enable it. To give Gemini permission to work inside apps, a small pop-up will appear after you give your command, where you can allow Gemini to proceed. You’ll have to do this for each app you want Gemini to use for you.

First-party vs. third-party app automations

Akshay Gangwar / Android Authority

As you’d expect, Google’s own services worked absolutely perfectly. It almost feels like the ideal future where you just delegate tasks, and they are handled for you without much back-and-forth. I’ve long used Google’s Spark, now called Gemini Tasks, to handle everyday Gmail responses, drafts, and changes inside Google Sheets without knowing every single one of those thousands of formulas. I frequently use it to watch for emails I’m expecting or chase stubborn customer support reps.

Since Workspace apps and other Google products (Photos, YouTube, et al.) are directly connected to Gemini on the backend using Connectors, the AI doesn’t need to use the consumer-facing interface to get the task done. A handful of third-party apps can also work in a similar fashion, including popular names like Spotify, Wispr Flow, Granola, Canva, and Adobe. However, on-screen automations open up a lot more third-party apps, and they are surprisingly less frustrating to use than those with connectors.

Once Gemini starts finding its way around the app, you can see it in action in a small window. While app automations are intended to offload your errands onto the AI while you focus on more important things, the novelty is so fascinating that I couldn’t help but gape at it in astonishment, as if watching an infant take its first steps.

I couldn't help but gape at it in astonishment, as if watching an infant take its first steps.

I started with Uber and asked it to find me a few options for the airport and tell me if the prices were unusually high. It followed the same flow that I manually would have: checked the available options and got back to me with all the details, including trip costs across vehicle options, which it confirmed didn’t include any surge prices. The results were similarly satisfactory when I asked it to add a few grocery items and repeat my coffee order from a few weeks ago on Blinkit and Zomato (equivalent to Instacart and DoorDash, respectively), though it required a bit of back-and-forth.

Do note that Gemini won’t make the final payment and will come back to you when it’s done with its part and ask you to review the final checkout page and make the payment. So, you don’t have to worry about AI wiping out your account (just yet). And on the preview page, you can either stop the automated task at any point or take over the screen if you think Gemini is running astray.

What worked and what didn’t

I started this test with a bit of skepticism because my experience with third-party connectors hasn’t been completely perfect. I’ve had to take back control because Gemini either didn’t understand what I wanted or required so much effort that it was easier to do it manually. Thankfully, on-screen automation has proven to be far more reliable in my testing — enough that I can delegate the task without actively reviewing it in real time, so I can shift my focus to other, more pressing things.

If I were to put a number to it, I would rate it 8 out of 10 because there were a few moments where it needed my intervention. The Uber experiment went quite well, except once when the phone froze during previewing, so we’ll put that aside, but while cross-checking an old order, it repeated the entire order instead of just the coffee I had asked it to. On another occasion, when I wanted to see if Zomato (a food ordering service) allowed scheduling, it had trouble scrolling up the wheel picker because its scroll gestures on the screen were far too long, something that we as humans intuitively know.

My biggest annoyance with the whole experience wasn't the automation feature itself, but the lack of continued conversation in Gemini for Android.

On another occasion, when filling up my cart with groceries, Gemini failed to add the right product or added replacements that I wouldn’t pick, which required me to ask it to search my order history and pick only the products that I frequently order, which again worked pretty well. More interestingly, if I couldn’t remember the specific name of a product, I could simply describe the packaging — like, “add the blue-colored milk carton that I frequently order” — and it would follow.

As you can tell, none of these are deal breakers but minor inconveniences that could easily be solved with a future update. In fact, I’m rather impressed by how nearly flawlessly everything works. Having said that, my biggest annoyance with the whole experience wasn’t the automation feature itself, but the lack of continued conversation in Gemini for Android. Each time Gemini returned the result, I had to switch on the mic to talk to it. Before you point it out, on-screen automations don’t work inside Gemini Live, at least they didn’t for me.

Did Gemini actually make my day easier?

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

I wish I was using the time when Gemini was working on the errand to do something else, but I was busy marveling at my phone automatically, almost magically, doing things. But I hope, as the novelty wears off, like it has with other AI tools I use to manage work on my desktop, it will prove to be a solid helping hand to take over the routine tasks that don’t require too much attention. Of course, I can still take over manually when, say, I’m ordering something different or special instead of repeating my past orders.

And with routine use of on-screen automation, I now understand the gaps that often require Gemini to follow up with me, like when something is out of stock or it adds extra dishes to my cart. I can add those restrictions or workarounds in my first prompt itself to minimize my manual interventions. And I’m sure, as Gemini learns more about my preferences, it will get even better at predicting them by itself, requiring me only at the checkout page for final confirmation and payment.

But even today in its current form, Gemini’s on-screen task automation has brought us closer to the Jarvis-like sci-fi reality, and I’m all for it.

The Roborock Saros 20 Flow is an expensive robot vacuum that's almost worth every penny

Incredible mopping and powerful suction, but at a very steep price.

The massive 36,000Pa suction power handles everyday cleaning with ease, and the overall experience is top-notch. The Roborock Saros 20 Flow ($1699.99 at Amazon) is one of the company’s most expensive robot vacuum cleaners, bringing major upgrades to mopping and hands-free maintenance, along with 36,000Pa suction. It’s also one of the most feature-packed robot vacuums I’ve tested in a while, with plenty that makes everyday cleaning a lot easier. But does it do enough to justify its hefty price tag and earn a spot among the best robot vacuums you can buy? Let’s find out.

There’s a lot going on with the Roborock Saros 20 Flow

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Roborock seems to have taken some inspiration from Qualcomm when it comes to naming its products (that’s how confusing the lineup is right now). There’s the Qrevo series of robot vacuums, the F25 series of cordless wet-dry vacuums, and then there’s the company’s flagship Saros 20 lineup, which currently includes three models: the Saros 20, the Saros 20 Flow, and the Saros 20 Sonic.

While all three are premium robot vacuums, the biggest difference is how they handle mopping. The regular Saros 20 uses traditional rotating mop pads, while the Saros 20 Sonic, which costs the same $1,699.99 as the Flow, uses a vibrating mop pad. The Saros 20 Flow, on the other hand, comes with a roller mop that’s designed to clean itself continuously as it moves across your floors.

In terms of design, the Saros 20 Flow looks much like any other premium robot vacuum. It has a circular body with two side brushes at the front, a roller mop at the back, and a retractable LiDAR sensor on top. Interestingly, despite having a retractable LiDAR sensor, the Saros 20 Flow is slightly taller than the regular Saros 20, measuring 3.54 inches compared to 3.14 inches. This means it might struggle to get underneath certain pieces of furniture that the regular model can reach, although I didn’t run into many issues with this during my testing.

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

The docking station is also quite large, but that’s because it handles most of the maintenance for you. There are two separate water tanks for clean and dirty water, a compartment for cleaning solution, and a dust bag that collects everything the vacuum picks up.

Thankfully, Roborock has made the initial setup straightforward. Most of the components come pre-installed, so all you really need to do is attach the base tray, plug in the power cord, and you’re good to go. Pairing the vacuum with your phone is just as easy. You simply scan the QR code on the unit, and the Roborock app takes care of the rest.

The roller mop is the real star of the show

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Coming back to the robot vacuum itself, one of the biggest highlights of the Saros 20 Flow is its roller mop. Unlike traditional robot vacuums that use rotating mop pads, the Saros 20 Flow uses a continuously rotating roller that gets cleaned with fresh water as it mops. This means the vacuum isn’t simply dragging the same dirty mop across your floors, which is particularly useful if you have a lot of hard flooring in your home.

The suction power is equally impressive, with the same 36,000Pa suction we saw on the Saros 20. It also features Roborock’s AdaptiLift Traverse 3.0 system, which allows the vacuum to raise its chassis and cross two-step thresholds up to a combined height of 8.8cm (3.46 inches), with the first step up to 4.5cm (1.77 inches). This helps if you have raised door thresholds or uneven flooring between rooms.

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

As for the actual cleaning experience, one thing that immediately stood out to me was just how quiet the Saros 20 Flow is. Despite having such powerful suction, it’s noticeably quieter than several other robot vacuums I’ve tested. Of course, it gets louder when you crank up the suction, but for everyday cleaning, I didn’t find the noise particularly bothersome.

I also like how little I had to intervene once everything was set up. The Roborock app uses AI to automatically determine the suction power, water usage, and cleaning sequence based on the room and how dirty the floor is. You can manually adjust all these settings whenever you want, but I found the automatic mode worked well for most cleaning sessions.

In terms of features, there is AI dirt detection onboard as well. This means the robot vacuum can automatically recognize dirty spots on the floor and go over them again if needed, without you having to tell it to do so.

Cleaning performance is excellent, with a few caveats

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

If there’s one thing I didn’t particularly like about the Saros 20 Flow’s cleaning performance, it’s the edge cleaning. The Saros 20 Flow has an extendable roller mop that moves out from the side of the robot vacuum to clean along walls and edges. However, I found the results to be a bit hit or miss.

There were several instances where the vacuum left certain spots unmopped or uncleaned, even when cleaning along a perfectly straight wall. It’s not a dealbreaker by any means, but it’s something I noticed more than once during my testing. That said, this is my biggest complaint after using the Saros 20 Flow for the past few weeks. If mopping is your priority and you have a lot of hard flooring in your home, the Saros 20 Flow is hard to beat.

As for battery life, I found it to be pretty good, especially considering the size of my home. I tested the Saros 20 Flow in a roughly 2,500-square-foot home with three bedrooms, a large living area, and plenty of furniture. During a full cleaning session, with vacuuming followed by mopping, the battery dropped to around 35% by the time it finished. That’s impressive considering how much ground it had to cover, and if you’re using it for occasional cleaning or have a smaller home, battery life shouldn’t be much of a concern.

The Roborock Saros 20 Flow cleaned my roughly 2,500-square-foot home with around 35% battery to spare.

The water tanks, however, are a different story. During the same cleaning session, I had to refill the clean water tank and empty the dirty water tank midway through. This will depend on how large your home is and how dirty the floors are, but it’s worth keeping in mind if you’re planning to use the vacuum in a similarly large space.

In terms of cleaning speed, the Saros 20 Flow took around three hours to completely clean my home. It’s worth noting that I used a cleaning cycle where the vacuum first cleaned the floors and then went over them again with the mop, rather than the default setting, which does both simultaneously. The overall cleaning time should be considerably shorter if you choose to vacuum and mop together.

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Another area where the Saros 20 Flow impressed me was obstacle avoidance. It can recognize different household objects and navigate around them without getting stuck. During my testing, it successfully identified shoes and loose cables on the floor and avoided them without any intervention. And yes, this also means that the Saros 20 Flow has a built-in camera that helps identify objects, and you can even enable an option in the Roborock app to capture photos of what it avoids.

There’s also a remote monitoring feature that lets you use the robot’s camera to check on your home. However, I didn’t end up using this feature because I don’t particularly want another surveillance camera inside my house.

Apart from occasionally dealing with the water tanks, the Saros 20 Flow pretty much takes care of itself.

Once the cleaning is done, the Saros 20 Flow automatically returns to its docking station and starts cleaning the roller mop. By default, the mop washing cycle is set to Balanced, but you can also choose a more intensive cleaning mode that uses water heated to as much as 100°C (212°F). This helps remove dirt and grime from the roller without you having to wash it manually.

After washing, the docking station also dries the mop using warm air over the next few hours. items.body: Next year's iPhone 20 Pro models will make extensive use of 3D-printed titanium in their frames, based on the latest rumor coming out of China. In a new post on Weibo, the leaker known as "Fixed Focus Digital" claims that Apple plans to manufacture parts of the device's mid-frame using a laser-based titanium powder 3D-printing process – one which would result in significantly improved durability. The leaker is apparently so confident in the accuracy of the rumour that they even suggested followers take screenshots of the Weibo post and reference it next year when the device is announced. Earlier this month, Fixed Focus Digital claimed that Apple would return to titanium for next year's 20th-anniversary iPhone models. The iPhone 18 Pro models currently use aluminum frames. Apple already uses the 3D-printing technique to produce the titanium cases of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and titanium Apple Watch Series 12 models, after the company debuted the process with the Ultra 3 and Series 11. Apple also uses it for the iPhone Air's USB-C port enclosure. The process involves using lasers to fuse successive layers of titanium powder. Apple says this allows for more complex structural designs than conventional manufacturing methods, and significantly reduces material waste. The technology could give Apple greater design flexibility as it develops its rumored all-glass 20th-anniversary iPhone design, which is expected to feature curved glass and virtually invisible display bezels . Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman has described the planned changes as the biggest overhaul of the Pro line since the iPhone X. What remains unclear is how Apple intends to address the thermal challenges associated with titanium, given the superior heat dissipation properties of the aluminum used in its current Pro models. Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 20 Pro series in the fall of 2027. Leakers have referred to the devices as the "iPhone 20 Pro," but Apple's actual naming plans are unknown. Tags: 20th-

6 simple tweaks I use to get two days of battery from my Galaxy Watch 9

Battery life continues to be a struggle for Galaxy Watch owners.

•

•

•

Rushil Agrawal / Android Authority

When the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 was first announced, one of the features that excited me most was the larger battery. I actually upgraded to a 44mm model, so I was expecting a significant improvement in battery life compared to my 40mm Watch 8. However, in practice, I found that it lasted roughly the same amount of time.

Even so, I don’t have to charge it daily, and that’s thanks to a handful of tweaks that get me two days instead. These tweaks balance usability with battery saving so that you don’t give up too many features in the quest to extend battery life.

Readers' poll

Do you think the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 delivers enough battery life?

0 votes

Turn off the Always On Display

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

When you set up the Galaxy Watch 9, the Always On Display (AOD) is enabled by default. However, this is by far the most battery-hungry feature. When I have it enabled, my watch needs to be charged daily. So if you’re like me and prefer to keep charging limited, this is the first setting you should change.

The difference in your battery life is apparent. After enabling the Always On Display for less than 30 minutes, it had already consumed 0.9% of my battery. Meanwhile, Samsung Health, which had been running for nearly 22 hours since the last charge, had only used 4.3% of my battery.

Disabling the AOD makes the biggest difference to your battery life without sacrificing much.

To disable the feature using your watch, swipe down and tap the watch icon.

You can also disable it in your Galaxy Wearable app:

1. Tap the hamburger icon at the bottom right.

2. Select Display > Always On Display. Make sure the toggle is turned off.

There are other ways to improve the battery life on your watch, but just disabling this feature will give you the largest gains.

Keep notifications limited to essential apps

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

The display is the biggest drain on your Watch 9’s battery, but background activity adds up too. That’s why I limit which apps I receive notifications from on my watch — it prevents my screen from waking unnecessarily, my watch doesn’t have to trigger vibrations as much, and it means I have fewer apps syncing in the background. I also only show notifications when my phone is not in use.

I always make sure to only enable notifications from the apps that are most important to me to reduce battery drain.

The app notifications you want to enable will depend on which apps you prioritize the most. I only want to see notifications from Slack, WhatsApp, Samsung Health, Google Calendar, and Google Messages. I’ve disabled everything else. I also make sure to manage notifications within each app so that I only receive alerts from certain channels or people, rather than large groups.

To manage the notifications you receive on your Watch 9:

1. Open Galaxy Wearable and select the hamburger icon at the bottom right.

2. Select Notifications > App notifications.

3. Toggle the apps you want to allow or disallow.

Under the Notifications panel, you can also select Show phone notifications on watch > Show alerts when not in use to only receive notifications when you’re not using your phone.

Uninstall unused apps

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

Even if you’re not using an app, it might still contribute to battery drain on your watch. I noticed this with an app I used to download Galaxy Watch 9 faces, even though I didn’t have a face from the app currently installed.

This is where the Galaxy Wearable’s Battery menu comes in handy. It lets you check which apps have used up battery power since your last charge. I recommend checking this tab to see if you have any unused apps draining your battery in the background.

Get rid of apps you're no longer using so that they don't contribute to battery drain.

You can access this menu in Galaxy Wearable using the following steps:

1. Tap the hamburger icon at the bottom right.

2. Go to Battery and scroll down to Usage since last full charge.

Here you can check which apps are the biggest culprits when it comes to battery drain.

To uninstall an app:

1. Select the hamburger icon > Apps.

2. Choose the app you want to uninstall from the list.

3. Tap the Uninstall button.

Choose a watch face with static elements

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

While you may be tempted to load your watch face with as much data as possible, along with animated visuals, doing so can drain more battery power. In fact, if you’re downloading a third-party watch face from the Google Play Store, the storefront now flags watch face apps that drain battery.

On third-party watch face storefronts like Facer, you will also see the impact a specific face has on battery life. Faces that sync a significant amount of data or that include animated visuals are usually the ones that impact battery life the most. Meanwhile, simple watch faces with few complications impact battery life the least.

Switching to an interactive, animated, or data-heavy watch face can reduce battery life.

Unfortunately, native Galaxy Watch faces don’t show details of the battery consumption of a specific watch face. In my own experience, switching from a Photos watch face to one that features Live wallpapers consumed more battery life. My Photos wallpaper consumed 0.6% of my watch’s battery life over 41 hours. The live wallpapers watch face consumed the same amount in 10 minutes after switching through five wallpapers.

Use a darker background

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

Even if you use a relatively static watch face, using a darker background also improves battery life. I tested this with my Photos watch face, switching from a light photo of my cats to a darker one featuring my black cat. I made the change after seeing the suggestion in the Galaxy Wearable app when choosing a watch face.

After switching to the darker background, I noticed that this added around four to five hours extra to my watch’s battery life. I also have Adaptive Brightness turned on so that my watch adjusts to the environment. While Adaptive Brightness didn’t make a massive difference on its own, it’s the type of tweak that you implement with other changes. These changes then add up and can add a considerable amount to your watch’s battery life.

Switch off Raise wrist to wake

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

Raise wrist to wake is another feature that drains battery life, but its effect will depend on how much you use the feature. When I disabled it, I got around another three hours of battery life. However, it was also an annoying change to make because it was so different from how I was used to using my watch.

I would recommend this change for people who don’t mind tapping their smartwatch to see notifications, or people who find that they accidentally trigger the feature fairly often. When I made all of these tweaks to my Galaxy Watch, I added an extra day to its battery life without sacrificing the health features that are important to me.

The changes you make will depend on the features that are most important to you.

A few other tricks that improve battery life include:

• Measuring heart rate every 10 minutes while still, rather than continuously.

• Switching to manual stress measurements.

• Turning off blood oxygen and skin temperature detection while sleeping.

• Turning off Auto detect workouts.

However, you’ll need to decide which features you’re willing to part with. I currently use heart rate monitoring every 10 minutes over continuous monitoring, but I keep blood oxygen and skin temperature detection enabled because I need them for the Vitals feature. Without the auto detection of workouts, I’d also forget to track my exercise completely. The best battery-saving tweaks for you will depend on what you use your watch for.

On third-party watch face storefronts like Facer, you will also see the impact a specific face has on battery life. Faces that sync a significant amount of data or that include animated visuals are usually the ones that impact battery life the most. Meanwhile, simple watch faces with few complications impact battery life the least.
Switching to an interactive, animated, or data-heavy watch face can reduce battery life.

Unfortunately, native Galaxy Watch faces don’t show details of the battery consumption of a specific watch face. In my own experience, switching from a Photos watch face to one that features Live wallpapers consumed more battery life. My Photos wallpaper consumed 0.6% of my watch’s battery life over 41 hours. The live wallpapers watch face consumed the same amount in 10 minutes after switching through five wallpapers.
Use a darker background

blocks.alt: Selecting a dark watch face on the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9.

blocks.text: Megan Ellis / Android Authority

Even if you use a relatively static watch face, using a darker background also improves battery life. I tested this with my Photos watch face, switching from a light photo of my cats to a darker one featuring my black cat. I made the change after seeing the suggestion in the Galaxy Wearable app when choosing a watch face.

After switching to the darker background, I noticed that this added around four to five hours extra to my watch’s battery life. I also have Adaptive Brightness turned on so that my watch adjusts to the environment. While Adaptive Brightness didn’t make a massive difference on its own, it’s the type of tweak that you implement with other changes. These changes then add up and can add a considerable amount to your watch’s battery life.
Switch off Raise wrist to wake

blocks.alt: The raise wrist to wake toggle on a Galaxy Watch 9.

blocks.text: Megan Ellis / Android Authority

Raise wrist to wake is another feature that drains battery life, but its effect will depend on how much you use the feature. When I disabled it, I got around another three hours of battery life. However, it was also an annoying change to make because it was so different from how I was used to using my watch.

I would recommend this change for people who don’t mind tapping their smartwatch to see notifications, or people who find that they accidentally trigger the feature fairly often. When I made all of these tweaks to my Galaxy Watch, I added an extra day to its battery life without sacrificing the health features that are important to me.
The changes you make will depend on the features that are most important to you.
A few other tricks that improve battery life include:

items: Measuring heart rate every 10 minutes while still, rather than continuously.
Switching to manual stress measurements.
Turning off blood oxygen and skin temperature detection while sleeping.
Turning off Auto detect workouts.

Mobile

We tested Samsung’s private Galaxy AI cloud on One UI 9.5 beta, and it made AI select smarter

Running AI select through Samsung SPAC on a Galaxy S26 Ultra produced an accurate calendar entry that didn't need edits.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 4:02 AM ET

•

•

Stephen Radochia / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• We got Samsung’s private AI cloud, referred to as “SPAC” in the code, working with AI select on a Galaxy S26 Ultra running One UI 9.5 Beta 1, producing more accurate calendar event extraction than its standard processing.

• Code references show SPAC supports Google’s Gemma 4 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6 (used in our test) and appears to route encrypted requests through a third-party relay to hide user identity.

• In our test, SPAC only pulled one event out of the five listed, but Samsung’s code indicates multi-event support. It also suggests photo editing, live translation, and writing tools could adopt SPAC next.

Yesterday, we reported that Samsung is building a private cloud for Galaxy AI. The system, called “SPAC” in Samsung’s code, appears to closely follow Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. At the time, SPAC wasn’t switched on for our Galaxy S26 Ultra. Now we’ve managed to get it running, and the result is better than what Galaxy AI does today.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

AI select used SPAC to add an event to our calendar

AI select, part of the Samsung Capture app, can pull details from your screen and suggest actions, like adding an event to your calendar. We pointed it at a Google search result listing upcoming Lollapalooza dates and tapped “Add event.”

On One UI 9.5 Beta 1 on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, this normally opens Samsung Calendar with fields filled in from the selected text.

The result was a bit of a mess: the event was titled “Course Reservation” for some reason. It selected the Mumbai entry for the dates but added multiple locations to the location field. Clearly, the “Lollapalooza India” context was lost.

Once we managed to turn on SPAC for AI select, the same selection and tap took a different route.

AI select sent the selection to Samsung’s SPAC servers, and after a few noticeable seconds of processing (which were missing before), Samsung Capture showed its own “Add event” sheet with a cleaner entry: “Lollapalooza India,” January 23, 2027, at Mahalaxmi Race Course, Mumbai. AI select managed to get the correct title, date, and venue for the calendar entry, without any edits from our end.

Admittedly, the result wasn’t perfect. The page listed five Lollapalooza editions, and SPAC returned only the first, possibly either because of our device location (Mumbai) or simply because it was the first entry in the list. Samsung’s code supports adding several events at once, so this could change by the time the feature goes live for users.

SPAC’s privacy design appears to be in place

SPAC’s code describes several privacy layers, including a third-party relay that hides where a request comes from and a public-style record of Samsung’s server software. When AI select used SPAC, our phone did not look up Samsung’s AI server directly. That’s pretty much how this design is supposed to work: the phone sends the request to a relay, and the relay forwards the encrypted request to SPAC, so the AI server only sees the request, not who sent it.

The code lists Google’s Gemma 4 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6 as AI select’s two SPAC options, and our test used Qwen 3.6. Your phone will only send the model’s name with the request, so we can’t confirm which model actually answered.

What this means for Galaxy AI

Stephen Radochia / Android Authority

The demo is small, but it’s the first sign that Samsung’s private AI cloud is real and not just code in the platform. A Galaxy phone can already send it a request and get a useful answer, although all of this is still very much a beta.

If Samsung goes ahead, AI select could be one of the first Galaxy AI features to run on SPAC, with photo editing, live translation, and writing tools possibly following. It’s also not clear yet whether SPAC-powered features would be free or paid as part of Galaxy AI Premium.

We’ve reached out to Samsung for comment on SPAC and will update this article if we hear back.

items.summary: From specific settings to alternative emulators, here's what you can try on your non-Snapdragon device.

Gaming

Got a MediaTek, Exynos, or Pixel device? Here are 11 tips for emulation

From specific settings to alternative emulators, here's what you can try on your non-Snapdragon device.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 4:00 AM ET

•

•

Nick Fernandez / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

There’s no shortage of emulators on Android, letting you play everything from Atari 2600 and NES games to PC and Nintendo Switch titles. We’ve even seen Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, and Switch 2 emulators in recent times.

It’s fair to say, though, that devices with Qualcomm Snapdragon chips are generally the best for emulation. Phones and handhelds with MediaTek, Google Tensor, or Samsung Exynos silicon often suffer from worse performance and compatibility with new emulators as a result. Thankfully, there are plenty of tips you can try if you’re struggling with emulation on your MediaTek-powered device, Exynos-toting Galaxy phone, or Google Pixel.

Readers' poll

What's the best tip for emulation on Android?

0 votes

1. Use Vulkan rather than OpenGL (or ANGLE)

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

One of the most enduring tips for running emulators on non-Snapdragon devices is to switch the graphics renderer from OpenGL to Vulkan. Vulkan generally performs better than OpenGL, so you should get a speed boost by making the switch. This isn’t always the case, but it’s still one of the first things you should try if you’re having performance problems in an emulator.

It’s also worth noting that Samsung’s and Google’s chips don’t have great OpenGL support in the first place. Instead, they use a “wrapper” called ANGLE to translate OpenGL calls to Vulkan. Some emulators offer ANGLE as an option in their settings. If an emulator doesn’t, you can enable ANGLE via developer options and leave the emulator on the OpenGL renderer. However, our own tests show that ANGLE can cause major issues on Pixel phones.

2. Turn down a few settings

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Is the emulated game running on your device, just slowly? Then there are several ways to speed it up. For one, you can try lowering the game’s rendering/internal resolution. This is usually set to 1x by default, but some emulators like ARMSX3 let you scale it down to 0.75x, 0.5x, and even 0.25x. The game will definitely look rougher as a result, but it’s worth a shot if your device’s GPU is taking a beating.

Another option worth pursuing in some emulators is frame skipping. As the name implies, this skips a certain number of frames (e.g., every other frame) so the game can keep running at closer to full speed. You can also try lowering the target frame rate if the game or emulator offers this option. After all, what’s the point of choosing 60fps if your device can’t maintain that frame rate in the first place?

3. Try an alternative emulator or fork

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

One of my favorite tips if you’re having emulator problems of any kind is to simply try a different emulator. AetherSX2 not running your favorite PS2 game? Then try NetherSX2 or ARMSX2. GameHub not running a specific PC game? You can always try GameNative, Winlator, or Winlator Ludashi.

There are limits to this approach, though. Some consoles only have one or two high-quality Android emulators, as is the case with the GameCube (Dolphin) and PSP (PPSSPP). Many advanced emulators also target Snapdragon-powered devices first, only improving support for MediaTek and other non-Snapdragon platforms down the line. Still, we highly recommend trying a different emulator if you’re having performance or compatibility problems.

It’s also worth noting that there are several forks of existing emulators that are optimized for MediaTek chips and other silicon. For example, we’ve seen MaliBridge and Winlator Mali for PC gaming, as well as XenDroid-Mali for Xbox 360 emulation. I’d urge caution before installing any unknown fork you come across, though.

4. Try emulating a different platform altogether

Trying to emulate a specific game, but it’s not working on your non-Snapdragon device? Switching to another emulator for the same platform is one option, but you could also try emulating a different platform altogether.

For example, a ton of games were released on both the PS2 and the original Xbox, and many of these titles also came to the GameCube. So if the PS2 version of a game isn’t giving you a great experience, you should definitely try the Xbox or GameCube version via HakuX or Dolphin, respectively.

This also applies to Xbox 360 and PS3 emulation. These consoles are still a pain to emulate on anything other than Snapdragon silicon, but some of their games came to PC as well. That means you might have better luck running these titles via GameNative, DroidDeck, or other PC “emulators.”

5. Use the system driver instead of Turnip

Robert Triggs / Android Authority

Custom Turnip drivers are all the rage in the emulation scene, as they deliver performance improvements and bug fixes over Qualcomm’s official GPU drivers. However, it’s worth stressing that Turnip drivers are only meant for Snapdragon-powered devices. You simply can’t use them on a phone, handheld, or tablet with a non-Snapdragon processor.

That’s why the team behind popular PC gaming app GameNative previously recommended sticking with the system driver instead of switching to Turnip on a MediaTek, Exynos, or Tensor device. This also applies to other emulators that support custom GPU drivers.

6. MediaTek users can try Vortek and PanVK

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Vivo X100 Ultra - Telephoto macro

Owners of non-Snapdragon devices can’t use custom Turnip drivers, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t similar options out there. Two of the most prominent are Vortek and PanVK, both of which target Mali GPUs.

The original creator of Winlator developed and released Vortek, a compatibility layer that sits on top of your device’s default graphics driver. GameNative and Winlator have previously integrated Vortek into their apps, and some users reported significant improvements on MediaTek devices. So it’s worth a shot if your emulator of choice supports it.

Meanwhile, PanVK has emerged as an alternative Vulkan driver for Mali graphics chips. We’ve seen a few PanVK projects, targeting everything from the budget Mali-G57 GPU to the Mali-G1 Ultra in recent flagship Dimensity chips. Neither Vortek nor PanVK appears to have had the same impact as Turnip did for Snapdragon chipsets, but they’re still worth trying in some emulators.

7. Exynos users can try the RADV driver

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Exynos users already had the ExynosTools suite, which is effectively a Vulkan translation layer for Exynos-powered Galaxy devices. But the open-source RADV driver arrived on Samsung Exynos devices earlier this month, too.

RADV for Samsung Xclipse is a port of the open-source Vulkan driver for AMD GPUs. Our own testing shows that this driver isn’t a silver bullet for Switch emulation, but it brought major performance gains in games like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. We’ve also seen online reports that the driver delivers fixes and performance improvements in some PC games. So add this to your list if you’ve got an Exynos-powered device.

8. Use MaliSX2 for PS2 games

ARMSX2 GitHub

NetherSX2 has long been the go-to PS2 emulator on Android, rising from the ashes of the abandoned AetherSX2. However, ARMSX2 has since arrived on Android and is arguably the best PS2 emulator on the platform. It recently debuted MaliSX2, which could be a game-changer for some users.

MaliSX2 is a Vulkan driver for devices with Mali GPUs, and it ships in ARMSX2 v2.8.3 and newer. You can find it by tapping Settings > Renderer, and the ARMSX2 team promises major boosts in some games. The team claimed that Ace Combat 4 and 5, which were previously unplayable with the stock driver, ran at full speed on a device with budget-tier Mali-G57 graphics.

This driver isn’t restricted to PS2 games, either. The team has confirmed that it’s coming to Dolphin and HakuX, although our own experience with a pre-release Dolphin build suggests MaliSX2 might not be an upgrade in some games just yet.

9. Try a native port instead of the emulated version

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

We’ve seen an explosion of games being unofficially ported to Android in 2026, largely thanks to generative AI. Everything from Skyrim and Need for Speed: Underground 2 to Donkey Kong Bananza and Tears of the Kingdom has been recompiled for mobile devices.

So it’s worth trying a native port of a game instead of emulating it. These unofficial ports still require you to supply the game ROM or ISO, though. We also have to caution that some vibe-coded “ports” are little more than an emulated game with a home screen icon, so you can’t expect better performance from these shoddy ports compared to the emulated version.

You should also be careful with these projects in general, as you’ll undoubtedly find bad actors spreading malware via dodgy ports. That said, I highly recommend checking the Gaming Emporium website for a regularly updated list of new Android ports.

10. Check Reddit for help

Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority

This sounds obvious, but you should definitely check Reddit to see if anyone has found solutions for emulating a specific console or game. It might just be a case of tweaking a couple of settings to get things running smoothly.

Subreddits worth checking include r/EmulationOnAndroid and r/EmulationMediatekMali. The latter is particularly great for getting help, but it’s also a showcase of games and emulators that run well on MediaTek hardware. So even if you’re not struggling with a specific title, it’s a good way to find games that are likely to run on your device.

11. Accept that you can’t run bleeding-edge emulators

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Even if you try every tip on this list, bleeding-edge emulators simply don’t play nicely with non-Snapdragon silicon. Just look at the first Switch 2 emulators, which generally don’t support MediaTek, Exynos, or Tensor chips.

It usually takes months (if not longer) for these projects to adequately support non-Snapdragon processors. So you’ll often have to accept that you can’t run that shiny new emulator straight away, no matter what you do.

It’s also worth noting that there are several forks of existing emulators that are optimized for MediaTek chips and other silicon. For example, we’ve seen MaliBridge and Winlator Mali for PC gaming, as well as XenDroid-Mali for Xbox 360 emulation. I’d urge caution before installing any unknown fork you come across, though.
4. Try emulating a different platform altogether

Trying to emulate a specific game, but it’s not working on your non-Snapdragon device? Switching to another emulator for the same platform is one option, but you could also try emulating a different platform altogether.

For example, a ton of games were released on both the PS2 and the original Xbox, and many of these titles also came to the GameCube. So if the PS2 version of a game isn’t giving you a great experience, you should definitely try the Xbox or GameCube version via HakuX or Dolphin, respectively.

This also applies to Xbox 360 and PS3 emulation. These consoles are still a pain to emulate on anything other than Snapdragon silicon, but some of their games came to PC as well. That means you might have better luck running these titles via GameNative, DroidDeck, or other PC “emulators.”
5. Use the system driver instead of Turnip
Robert Triggs / Android Authority

Custom Turnip drivers are all the rage in the emulation scene, as they deliver performance improvements and bug fixes over Qualcomm’s official GPU drivers. However, it’s worth stressing that Turnip drivers are only meant for Snapdragon-powered devices. You simply can’t use them on a phone, handheld, or tablet with a non-Snapdragon processor.

That’s why the team behind popular PC gaming app GameNative previously recommended sticking with the system driver instead of switching to Turnip on a MediaTek, Exynos, or Tensor device. This also applies to other emulators that support custom GPU drivers.
6. MediaTek users can try Vortek and PanVK

blocks.alt: Vivo X100 Ultra Dimensity chip 3.7x resized

blocks.text: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority
Vivo X100 Ultra - Telephoto macro

Owners of non-Snapdragon devices can’t use custom Turnip drivers, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t similar options out there. Two of the most prominent are Vortek and PanVK, both of which target Mali GPUs.

The original creator of Winlator developed and released Vortek, a compatibility layer that sits on top of your device’s default graphics driver. GameNative and Winlator have previously integrated Vortek into their apps, and some users reported significant improvements on MediaTek devices. So it’s worth a shot if your emulator of choice supports it.

Meanwhile, PanVK has emerged as an alternative Vulkan driver for Mali graphics chips. We’ve seen a few PanVK projects, targeting everything from the budget Mali-G57 GPU to the Mali-G1 Ultra in recent flagship Dimensity chips. Neither Vortek nor PanVK appears to have had the same impact as Turnip did for Snapdragon chipsets, but they’re still worth trying in some emulators.
7. Exynos users can try the RADV driver
Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Exynos users already had the ExynosTools suite, which is effectively a Vulkan translation layer for Exynos-powered Galaxy devices. But the open-source RADV driver arrived on Samsung Exynos devices earlier this month, too.

RADV for Samsung Xclipse is a port of the open-source Vulkan driver for AMD GPUs. Our own testing shows that this driver isn’t a silver bullet for Switch emulation, but it brought major performance gains in games like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. We’ve also seen online reports that the driver delivers fixes and performance improvements in some PC games. So add this to your list if you’ve got an Exynos-powered device.
8. Use MaliSX2 for PS2 games
ARMSX2 GitHub

NetherSX2 has long been the go-to PS2 emulator on Android, rising from the ashes of the abandoned AetherSX2. However, ARMSX2 has since arrived on Android and is arguably the best PS2 emulator on the platform. It recently debuted MaliSX2, which could be a game-changer for some users.

MaliSX2 is a Vulkan driver for devices with Mali GPUs, and it ships in ARMSX2 v2.8.3 and newer. You can find it by tapping Settings > Renderer, and the ARMSX2 team promises major boosts in some games. The team claimed that Ace Combat 4 and 5, which were previously unplayable with the stock driver, ran at full speed on a device with budget-tier Mali-G57 graphics.

This driver isn’t restricted to PS2 games, either. The team has confirmed that it’s coming to Dolphin and HakuX, although our own experience with a pre-release Dolphin build suggests MaliSX2 might not be an upgrade in some games just yet.
9. Try a native port instead of the emulated version

blocks.alt: Halo unofficial port on cheap phone

blocks.text: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

We’ve seen an explosion of games being unofficially ported to Android in 2026, largely thanks to generative AI. Everything from Skyrim and Need for Speed: Underground 2 to Donkey Kong Bananza and Tears of the Kingdom has been recompiled for mobile devices.

So it’s worth trying a native port of a game instead of emulating it. These unofficial ports still require you to supply the game ROM or ISO, though. We also have to caution that some vibe-coded “ports” are little more than an emulated game with a home screen icon, so you can’t expect better performance from these shoddy ports compared to the emulated version.

You should also be careful with these projects in general, as you’ll undoubtedly find bad actors spreading malware via dodgy ports. That said, I highly recommend checking the Gaming Emporium website for a regularly updated list of new Android ports.
10. Check Reddit for help
Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority

This sounds obvious, but you should definitely check Reddit to see if anyone has found solutions for emulating a specific console or game. It might just be a case of tweaking a couple of settings to get things running smoothly.

Subreddits worth checking include r/EmulationOnAndroid and r/EmulationMediatekMali. The latter is particularly great for getting help, but it’s also a showcase of games and emulators that run well on MediaTek hardware. So even if you’re not struggling with a specific title, it’s a good way to find games that are likely to run on your device.
11. Accept that you can’t run bleeding-edge emulators

blocks.alt: XenDroid Xbox 360 emulator running on Android handheld scaled

blocks.text: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Even if you try every tip on this list, bleeding-edge emulators simply don’t play nicely with non-Snapdragon silicon. Just look at the first Switch 2 emulators, which generally don’t support MediaTek, Exynos, or Tensor chips.

It usually takes months (if not longer) for these projects to adequately support non-Snapdragon processors. So you’ll often have to accept that you can’t run that shiny new emulator straight away, no matter what you do.

Morphe v2.4.0 beats Google to bringing YouTube videos to your Android Auto screen

It only shows up when your vehicle is parked.

TL;DR

• Morphe v2.4.0 is out, and it adds support for playing YouTube videos on Android Auto and other in-car entertainment platforms.

• YouTube shows up in the Android Auto launcher when the car is parked.

• Along with this, Morphe’s version of YouTube and YouTube Music also get a host of playability improvements.

Morphe is a popular open-source tool for modding popular Android apps to add features and remove ads from YouTube, YouTube Music, and other media streaming apps. In the last major update, it added 4K video downloads, surpassing download-quality limits even on the official YouTube app. Now, it’s out with another update that brings a host of changes to patched versions of Reddit, YouTube, and YouTube Music. One that truly stands out — and we hope isn’t blocked by Google — is the ability to play YouTube videos on Android Auto.

Release notes for version 2.40 of the Morphe app say a new patch now lets Morphe YouTube be seen as a “parked video app.” As a result, the app shows up in Android Auto’s app drawer, and you can watch videos directly while your vehicle isn’t moving. This is currently only available as an early access feature and also works with DriveDeck. Google itself has been working to bring a similar functionality to phones running Android 17 or newer by the end of the year. Currently, users can only listen to audio from YouTube videos on Android Auto, but the app must be controlled from the phone.

Meanwhile, another patch detects when the YouTube app is projected onto the car’s display and adjusts its layout for horizontal screens, while another one hides the navigation bar to utilize the space better. It also enables Android Auto alternatives such as DriveDeck, Gearslip, AARE, and Flywheel to browse YouTube Music’s library.

Along with this, the latest Morphe update brings several minor upgrades to both YouTube and YouTube Music that aren’t specific to Android Auto. These improvements include a new Ghost mode, similar to Incognito, where watched videos don’t show in your watch history or impact your recommendations. You can browse using Ghost mode for an entire session or launch just one video using the three-dot button — all this without having to sign out of your account.

Lyrics in YouTube Music now support a full-screen mode, along with support for custom fonts. You also get the option to disable gestures for changing tracks by swiping over the album art. Besides this, YouTube Music also gains a direct Sonos casting button that lets you stream audio directly to UPnP speakers from Sonos and other brands, so long as they’re on the same Wi-Fi.

TL;DR

• OPPO has introduced three monthly AI subscription tiers for ColorOS 17 in India.

• The plans range from around $3 to $10 and will offer up to 100,000 credits per month.

• Only Live Translation, AI Photo Agent, and Transcription features will use credits, while other AI features remain free.

OnePlus recently confirmed that it will start imposing usage limits on some AI features in ColorOS 17. Users will have a free usage allowance, after which they can either pay for more usage or wait for their allowance to reset. However, the company hadn’t confirmed price details just yet. Well, we’re getting a clearer idea of its plans now.

According to a post on X by user Ashok Mor, OPPO has started offering subscription-based AI plans for ColorOS 17. There are three subscription tiers, per their post:

• Basic: Rs. 289/month (~$3/month) for 20,000 credits

• Pro: Rs. 579/month (~$6/month) for 50,000 credits

• Ultra: Rs. 959/month (~$10/month) for 100,000 credits

These credits are reportedly shared across three AI features: Live Translation, AI Photo Agent, and Transcription. Based on the post, the Basic plan will get you roughly 50 Photo Agent uses or 100 minutes of translation. The Pro plan bumps that up to 125 uses or 250 minutes, while the Ultra plan offers around 250 uses or 500 minutes.

@_techibee / X

You can also buy top-up credits if you run out of your monthly quota, with credit packs starting at Rs. 189 (~$2) for 10,000 credits. These credits are valid for one year. OPPO also seems to be running a limited-time offer that gives users 10,000 free credits per month for one year, so users can experiment with the AI features before deciding whether to subscribe.

Based on the screenshots in the post, it seems only the three AI features listed above will use AI credits. Other AI features in ColorOS 17 could remain available for free, at least for now. Neither OnePlus nor OPPO has officially announced a rollout or confirmed pricing for other regions. We have reached out to both companies for a statement and will update this post when we hear back.

Wearables and health

Oura is dropping Android 11 support in December, and users risk losing health data

Upgrading after the deadline won't bring back your health history.

•

•

•

Kaitlyn Cimino / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Oura will officially drop support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026.

• Users who don’t upgrade to Android 12 or newer by the deadline risk losing their historical health data.

• Those who remain on Android 11 may retain access to some limited historical app features.

One of the biggest benefits of wearing an Oura Ring is that the longer you use it, the more you learn about your health. From personalized annual health recaps to long-term blood pressure trends, many of Oura’s features become more useful as you build up months or even years of health data. However, some Android users could soon lose access to that history simply because of the phone they use.

Oura has updated its Android software updates support page to reveal that it will discontinue support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026. Starting on that date, you’ll need a phone running Android 12 or newer to continue enjoying the full Oura app experience.

Oura will drop support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026. If you are using an Android device, be sure to update to Android 12 or higher to ensure no loss of data or features. If you decide not to upgrade, you may still be able to use some limited historical Oura App features. Please note that if you do upgrade your smartphone system later, your historical Oura data will not carry over.

What’s particularly concerning is that this goes beyond missing out on new features and app updates. Oura warns that users who stick with Android 11 may retain access to some limited historical app features, but upgrading their phone’s operating system later will not bring their historical Oura data with them.

Essentially, putting off that software update could cost you years of sleep, activity, and recovery history.

Android 11 is now more than six years old, and Oura isn’t alone in moving away from older Android versions. Earlier this month, Google raised Android Auto’s minimum requirement to Android 11. But Oura is taking things a step further.

If your phone is still running Android 11, you should check for available software updates before December 8. Those whose phones are no longer eligible for OS updates may need to switch to a newer device. Oura also lets you export your health data through its Membership Hub, so it’s worth downloading a copy before the deadline.

items.summary: This charging reminder feature could even refer to your calendar entries for more personalized alerts.

Samsung phones can soon nudge you when you miss your usual charging window

This charging reminder feature could even refer to your calendar entries for more personalized alerts.

•

•

•

Ryan Haines / Android Authority

TL;DR

• Samsung’s One UI 9.5 beta can apparently tell you when you’ve missed your usual charging time.

• This alert will show up in the Settings menu and will also show how many hours of battery life you have left.

• This feature could be very useful if you’re forgetful or busy.

Samsung recently launched the One UI 9.5 beta program, allowing Galaxy S26 owners to get their hands on the latest software before the stable release. We’ve already uncovered plenty of features, but it looks like the company has a convenient charging-related feature up its sleeve.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

We’ve dug into the Device Care app (v13.9.00.12) in One UI 9.5 and discovered that Samsung phones could soon issue an alert when you’ve missed your usual charging time. We can confirm that this alert will appear when the battery is at 20-30% capacity, your phone isn’t charging, and power-saving modes are disabled. Check out the string below.

Code

<string name="suggest_appbar_charging_description">You missed your usual charging time.</string>

We’ve also uncovered strings (seen below) which show that the alert could use events in your default calendar for context. More specifically, the alert could mention that your battery might be low for a workout, movie, meeting, or show/concert at a given time. If you don’t have a matching calendar event, then the feature will fall back to the alert message seen in the string above.

Code

<string name="suggest_appbar_exercise_description">Battery may be low for your workout at %s.</string> 
<string name="suggest_appbar_meeting_description">Battery may be low for your meeting at %s.</string> 
<string name="suggest_appbar_movie_description">Battery may be low for your movie at %s.</string> 
<string name="suggest_appbar_performance_description">Battery may be low for your %1$s at %2$s.</string>

So how does this actually work? Well, you’ll first need to enable Samsung’s personalized suggestions option and have a device with One UI 9.5. The phone will then identify your preferred charging window by learning from four weeks of charging history, as retained by the Smart suggestions app. The device will then check if the current hour falls within this preferred charging window, and display the alert if this is the case. The code suggests that if you dismiss the alert, it won’t come back again for 24 hours, even if all other conditions are met. Oddly enough, we also found evidence that Samsung can remotely turn off this card.

There’s no country check, while the evidence we’ve uncovered also suggests that it won’t be exclusive to the Galaxy S27 series. So this charging alert could potentially come to older Galaxy phones in many markets.

What could these charging alerts look like?

SamMobile also posted a screenshot showing off this alert. It’s unclear whether this feature is available in some capacity or if the outlet manually enabled it by tinkering with the software. Check out the image below.

SamMobile

This notification apparently pops up at the top of the Settings menu. It also includes a graphic showing how many hours of battery life you have left and how much usage time you’ll gain if you enable battery-saving mode.

I can see this proactive alert being very useful for people who either forget to charge their phones or those who are very busy. That battery life graphic should also help you make up your mind about whether you need to charge your device straight away.

Either way, this charging alert seems like a very sensible addition to One UI 9.5. We hope other Android OEMs copy Samsung and implement this in their own software skins.

TCL CSOT showed off the future of display tech at DTC 2026.
